opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more interesting developments of the last couple of years. For a long time, the dominant story about progress in AI was about scaling training compute: you make the model bigger, train it on more data, spend more FLOP during pre-training, and capabilities improve fairly predictably. What we've started to appreciate more recently is that there's a second axis you can scale, which is how much compute you spend when the model is actually being used, at inference time.

The basic idea is that instead of having the model produce an answer in a single forward pass, you let it think longer. It can generate a long chain of reasoning, try multiple approaches, check its own work, sample many candidate solutions and pick the best one using some verifier, and so on. On a lot of tasks, especially ones with a clear notion of correctness like math, coding, or certain scientific problems, performance keeps improving as you give the model more of this inference budget.

One way I like to think about it is in terms of a trade-off between training compute and inference compute. There's earlier work, for example on game-playing systems like those for board games and poker, showing you can often substitute one for the other: a smaller model that searches or deliberates more can match a larger model that searches less. Language models seem to show a similar pattern. So in some regimes you can get the equivalent of a substantial increase in training compute by spending more at inference time. That doesn't mean they're perfectly interchangeable, and the exchange rate varies a lot by task, but the existence of that trade-off is important.

I think it matters for a few reasons. First, it suggests that capabilities at any given moment may be somewhat underestimated if you only look at the model answering quickly. If someone is willing to pay for a lot of inference, they can unlock noticeably stronger performance from the same underlying weights. Second, it changes the economics. Training is a big upfront fixed cost, whereas inference scales with usage, so you get a different cost structure, and potentially much more flexibility to spend heavily on problems that are especially valuable. Third, it interacts with training itself: you can use expensive inference to generate high-quality reasoning traces or solutions, then train on those, which is a kind of bootstrapping loop. That's part of why the reasoning models have improved so quickly.

There are limits, of course. Returns tend to diminish, often roughly logarithmically, so you need exponentially more inference compute for steady gains. It works best where answers can be verified, and it's less clear how far it goes on open-ended tasks without a good feedback signal. And if the underlying model just lacks some knowledge or capability, thinking longer won't necessarily conjure it up.

But overall I see it as a genuine new scaling dimension, not just a trick. And from the perspective of forecasting AI progress, it means we have to keep track of both how much compute goes into training and how much is available, and economically worthwhile, to deploy at inference. That second quantity could become very large as AI systems get deployed more broadly and are trusted with longer, more complex tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says training and inference compute can substitute for one another, and that a smaller model spending more at inference can match a larger model that spends less.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify Epoch’s 2022 prediction or state the specific tenfold-to-hundredfold equivalence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think inference scaling is genuinely one of the more important developments in the last couple of years, but I'd want to be careful about how we think about it, because there's a lot of confusion about what it actually buys you.

So the basic observation is that you can get better performance from a model not just by training a bigger model on more data, but by letting it think longer at test time, generating more tokens, sampling many candidate solutions and selecting among them, doing search, that kind of thing. And the striking thing from the work OpenAI and others have published is that you get fairly clean log-linear improvements in performance as you scale up the amount of compute used at inference, at least on certain domains like math and coding where you have verifiable answers.

Now, the way I'd frame this is that inference compute and training compute are, to some extent, substitutes. You can trade off between them. There's been some nice work showing that for a given problem, a smaller model with a lot of test-time compute can match a much larger model with less. And that's economically important because it changes the cost structure. Training is a one-time fixed cost that you amortize across all your queries, whereas inference is a variable cost you pay every time. So if you can shift capability into inference, you can be more flexible about where you spend.

But I think there are a few caveats that matter a lot. The first is that the gains from scaling inference seem to be quite domain dependent. Where you have a clear reward signal, where you can check whether an answer is correct, you can do a lot. It's much less obvious that it transfers to tasks that are open-ended, where there's no verifier, where the model has to exercise judgment in a way that's hard to score. That might change, people are working on it, but as of now the evidence is strongest in the verifiable domains.

The second caveat is about the magnitude. When you look at how much inference compute you'd need to match a jump in training compute, it's often enormous. If you're spending ten or a hundred times more per query, that's fine for a research benchmark, but it starts to matter for deployment at scale. So it's not the case that inference scaling replaces training scaling. I think they're complementary, and the labs that do best are going to be the ones that push both frontiers.

And then the third thing, which I think is actually the most interesting from a forecasting perspective, is that the two reinforce each other. If you have a model that can produce better outputs by thinking longer, you can use those better outputs as training data for the next model. You distill the test-time search back into the weights. And so inference scaling isn't just a way to get more out of a fixed model, it's also a way of generating higher-quality training signal, which feeds back into the training side. That loop is, I think, a big part of why progress on reasoning has been faster than many people expected.

So the way I'd summarize it is, inference scaling has opened up a new axis along which you can push capabilities, and it's a real one, but it's not a free lunch. It's bounded by cost, it's currently concentrated in domains with good verifiers, and its biggest effect might end up being indirect, through the way it accelerates the training loop rather than through raw test-time performance alone.

r001.rationale: It says inference and training compute are substitutes and that a smaller model with much more test-time compute can match a much larger model with less.

r002.rationale: It mentions that matching a training-compute increase may require ten or a hundred times more inference compute, but does not identify this as Epoch’s 2022 prediction.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic idea is that there are two different places where you can spend compute to improve a model’s performance. One is during training, where you’re changing the model’s weights. The other is at inference time, where you’re using a trained model to work on a particular problem.

In the simplest case, you might have the model generate several possible solutions and then try to select the best one. Or you could have it break a problem into steps, check its work, and revise its answer. That gives you a way to trade additional computation for a better result without training a larger model.

The exciting possibility is that, for difficult problems, a model could spend much more time thinking than it does in an ordinary chatbot interaction. You wouldn’t necessarily want that for every question, but you might be willing to pay quite a lot for additional computation if you’re solving an important scientific or engineering problem.

The key uncertainty is how effectively models can use that extra compute. Generating more text doesn’t automatically mean making more progress. You need some way to explore useful alternatives and recognize when you’ve found a better answer. That’s easier in settings where you can check the result, like certain mathematics or programming tasks, and harder where evaluating an answer is itself difficult.

So I see inference compute as a potentially important additional dimension of scaling. But the strength of that opportunity depends on whether we can develop methods that reliably turn more computation at inference time into better reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts training-time and inference-time compute and says extra inference compute may improve results, but it does not state that this can compensate for reduced training compute while preserving the same performance.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Epoch’s 2022 prediction or the claimed tenfold-to-hundredfold equivalence to increased training compute.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic idea is that we can improve a model’s performance not just by spending more compute training it, but also by letting it do more work when answering a question. Instead of producing the first answer that comes to mind, it might explore several approaches, check intermediate steps, or revise an initial solution.

That gives us another dimension along which to scale. You can imagine keeping the model’s weights fixed but allowing it to spend seconds, minutes, or potentially much longer working on a difficult problem. The interesting question is how reliably that additional computation translates into better answers.

One important consideration is whether the model can recognize progress. In mathematics or programming, you sometimes have a relatively clear way to check a proposed solution. That makes searching over possible answers more useful. For more open-ended questions, generating more reasoning doesn’t necessarily help if the model can’t distinguish a good answer from a convincing mistake.

So I see substantial potential here, but I wouldn’t assume that simply letting a model run longer produces arbitrarily better performance. We need methods that make productive use of that extra compute, and we need to understand how quickly the gains diminish. If those methods work well, inference compute could become a major driver of capability alongside training compute.
